https://www.politico.eu/article/poland-p.text: Poland’s opposition is shifting further to the right ahead of an election next year and that threatens to have a major impact for the EU and Ukraine. The nationalist Law and Justice party (PiS) that ran the country from 2015 to 2023 — picking repeated battles with Brussels over rule of law and LGBTQ+ rights — split last Friday . At its heart, the feud centers on a clash between iron-fisted party leader Jarosław Kaczyński and former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki. The big question is what that rupture means for the political trajectory of a country that has one of the largest militaries in NATO and has been a key strategic ally to Kyiv since the Russian invasion. Advertisement Advertisement Allies of pro-EU Prime Minister Donald Tusk read it as good news. When Kaczyński stepped to the microphone to kick out Morawiecki, two lawmakers from Tusk’s governing coalition filmed themselves watching the speech, eating popcorn . You can see why they might be happy. Before the split, POLITICO’s Poll of Polls put Tusk’s Civic Coalition at 32 percent support and PiS at 26 percent. PiS has now slumped to 22 percent. But that is hardly the whole story. The combined forces of right-wing parties are still in a strong position if they team up for the 2027 election. And Friday’s split means that PiS is more likely to veer right in its alliances, choosing ideological consolidation over an attempt to win back the center. The wing of PiS led by Morawiecki had argued the party needed to broaden its appeal and adopt a less combative approach toward Brussels. Kaczyński instead appears determined to recapture voters who have defected further right. It is far from certain, however, how successfully Poland’s far-right parties can agree on a common agenda with PiS. Among the potential beneficiaries of Friday’s split are parties that oppose Ukraine joining the European Union — and, in the case of Grzegorz Braun’s Federation of the Polish Crown movement, advocate taking Poland out of the bloc altogether. Advertisement Advertisement Poland votes in the fall of 2027. On current polling, most plausible routes to a right-wing majority would require the Konfederacja party, Braun’s party or both. “For years, a right-wing voter in Poland had no alternative. If you had right-wing views, you voted for Law and Justice, because there was nothing else,” said Anna Bryłka, a member of the European Parliament and vice-president of Konfederacja, the biggest of the hard-right parties now gaining sway. “Today that alternative exists. Law and Justice is simply losing its hegemony on the right.” The breakup came to a head over a midnight deadline to renounce the faction Morawiecki had built inside the party, or leave. About 45 lawmakers refused to sign . Kaczyński declared them outside the party, triggering PiS’s most serious rupture in two decades. Mateusz Morawiecki is pictured during a summit in the European Parliament in Brussels on Feb. 3, 2026. | Thierry Monasse/Getty Images Morawiecki, prime minister until 2023, was hardly a centrist by European standards. But within PiS, his supporters represented a more economically liberal and tactically less confrontational camp — and a rival center of power. Yet PiS is bleeding voters rightward anyway. Kaczyński selected hardline former Education Minister Przemysław Czarnek as his preferred candidate for prime minister to win back Konfederacja’s electorate. The polls slid regardless . “Why would a voter choose the copy,” Bryłka said, “when they can vote for the original?” Advertisement Advertisement The kingmakers name their price In surveys testing a separate Morawiecki list, support for PiS falls to between 16 and 22 percent , Konfederacja takes roughly 13 to 15 percent and Braun’s party about 10 percent. Morawiecki’s Rozwój Plus (Development Plus) project has backing ranging from below the 5 percent parliamentary threshold to around 7.5 percent. No party with such weak support can govern alone. Bryłka’s conditions for forming a right-wing alliance hinge on Brussels: There must be no more transfer of powers to the EU, no softening on the climate policy that her party has opposed since 2019, and a firm “no” to Ukraine’s membership of the EU. Even Braun, whom Kaczyński has called too toxic for any coalition, is not beyond the pale for her party. “We maintain good relations,” said Michał Wawer, Konfederacja’s treasurer and a member of the national parliament. “We are ready for cooperation in government in the future, if the majority works out that way.” Morawiecki’s camp has ruled that out. “Not a chance,” said Paweł Jabłoński, a former deputy foreign minister expelled with Morawiecki. Braun’s party, he added, “is destructive.” Others in PiS are less categorical. “There is no enemy on the right,” Kaczyński loyalist Jacek Sasin told reporters Friday, floating “some form of non-aggression pact.” The real enemy, he added, was Tusk’s coalition. Advertisement Advertisement Can the right unite? For all the acrimony, Morawiecki’s breakway camp is not looking across the aisle. Jabłoński said his group wants to keep cooperating with PiS, and ruled out any deal with Tusk — whose coalition, he said, remains the opponent. The one figure who could reach across the splintered right and unify it is President Karol Nawrocki, elected last year with the support of PiS and Konfederacja voters — and talk of a single right-wing list under his presidential umbrella has circulated in Warsaw for months. Kaczyński has embraced a version of the idea. Karol Nawrocki speaks during doorstep statements as part of the NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey on July 8, 2026. | Altan Gocher/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images “We are working to win the election, to unite as large a part of the right as possible, so that we go on one list,” he said in June — provided Konfederacja drops its hostility toward PiS. Braun, he made clear, would not be invited. “Only Karol Nawrocki can sort this out,” Bryłka said. “He could be the patron of some reconciliation between Jarosław Kaczyński and Prime Minister Morawiecki” — a reconciliation she expects to happen sooner or later anyway. “The question is whether he wants that role,” she added. “He has all the tools — and everything suggests he does.” Advertisement Advertisement Not that governing would be simple. Building a coalition of three parties is difficult enough, Bryłka said. “From four, it’s a genuinely complicated process.” Her forecast for the next parliament? “Chaos.” But even a fragmented right would not automatically save Tusk. In one poll conducted by IBRiS , the combined support of the right-wing parties did not fall after the PiS rupture. It edged up, from 47.5 percent to 47.9 percent. The voters leaving Kaczyński appear to be shopping elsewhere on the right, not crossing over to Tusk. Meanwhile, the prime minister’s own coalition is fraying: Of his governing partners, only the Left is consistently polling above the threshold required to enter parliament. Tusk’s likeliest path to survival is the right wasting its own votes. If Morawiecki runs independently and falls below the 5 percent threshold, his supporters’ ballots would win no seats. Konfederacja is candid about the risk that would pose to the entire right. “Those 4 percent of lost votes could decide what the majority looks like,” Wawer said. Tusk has been sounding less cheerful than the lawmakers with the popcorn. “I won’t cry for Law and Justice,” he told reporters Monday, “but there is certainly nothing to celebrate.” Advertisement

https://www.straitstimes.com/world/europ.text: Fire effects cleared up at Russian port of Ust-Luga after drone attack, governor says Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox Published Aug 14, 2026, 11:50 AM Updated Aug 14, 2026, 02:35 PM Set as preferred source Listen Aug 14 - Russian authorities quickly cleared up damage on Friday from a fire at the Baltic Sea port of Ust-Luga, a major hub for oil exports, that had been triggered by a Ukrainian drone attack, regional governor Alexander Drozdenko said. Ukraine has been striking targets within Russia, from ports and refineries to commercial warehouses, in a bid to raise the costs for Moscow of pursuing the full-scale war it launched in 2022. "All consequences of the attack in the port of Ust-Luga have been cleared up," Drozdenko posted on Russian messaging service MAX. "There were no casualties." He gave no further details. Earlier, Drozdenko said more than 50 drones were downed overnight in the northern region around St Petersburg. More than a dozen major refineries have been hit, some of them repeatedly, causing widespread fuel shortages. The governor of the Tver region northwest of Moscow reported another attack overnight on a warehouse of online retailer Wildberries, whose sites have been targeted more than 20 times in the past month. Debris from "enemy drones" damaged the wall of the facility but there were no injuries, he said. Also in the Baltic region on Friday, fighter jets shot down a drone that entered the airspace of NATO and EU member Latvia, its armed forces said, while Finland temporarily curbed movement in parts of the Baltic Sea to guard against drone attacks. https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Kate Wilson, an activist who was deceived into a relationship with an undercover police officer said: ‘We may never understand the full extent of the misconduct that has occurred in undercover policing’. Photograph: Jordi Matas/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Kate Wilson, an activist who was deceived into a relationship with an undercover police officer said: ‘We may never understand the full extent of the misconduct that has occurred in undercover policing’. Photograph: Jordi Matas/The Guardian Spycops scandal Undercover police and policing Victims say Home Office attempt to curtail spycops inquiry will result in a ‘cover-up’ Shabana Mahmood is concerned about length and £144m cost of inquiry into intrusive police surveillance Rob Evans Sun 20 Sep 2026 04.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 04.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Victims of intrusive police surveillance have accused the government of seeking to cut short the spycops public inquiry that has been examining widespread misconduct committed by undercover officers. The independent judge-led inquiry is scrutinising how officers, who spied on tens of thousands of political activists over more than four decades, carried out abuses such as deceiving women into sexual relationships and fathering children. The inquiry has been running for more than a decade, and is expected to last another two years. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has said she is concerned about the length and cost of the process. It was set up in 2015 and was supposed to have been completed within three years. Latest figures show the inquiry, which has been led by retired judge Sir John Mitting, has so far cost £144m . Mahmood initiated a public consultation, which closes on Sunday, that she said would help determine whether the inquiry should continue in a different format. However, those who were spied on say that the Home Office is looking to severely limit or scrap the later stages, leaving the full extent of wrongdoing by the police hidden. They say more than 2,000 people have objected to what they believe would be a cover-up. The Home Office must not be allowed to bury the spycops inquiry | Imran Khan Read more The spycops inquiry is one of the longest-running public inquiries. According to the House of Commons , the longest in modern times was an inquiry into a sectarian murder in Northern Ireland which reported last week, 22 years after being commissioned. It has so far been investigating the Special Demonstration Squad (SDS) , a Metropolitan police unit that infiltrated political groups between 1968 and 2008. The inquiry has heard how the SDS officers formed long-term relationships with women without disclosing to them their true identity, spied on grieving families such as the parents of murdered teenager Stephen Lawrence , stole the identities of dead children and lied in court hearings . It is due to examine a second undercover squad, the National Public Order Intelligence Unit, which infiltrated political groups between 1999 and 2011. One of the unit’s key undercover officers was Mark Kennedy who infiltrated environmental and left-wing groups for six years. He deceived a large, but unknown, number of women into intimate relationships. Environmental campaigners had their criminal convictions overturned because crucial evidence gathered by Kennedy was withheld from their trials . The inquiry is also scheduled to look at the case of an undercover police officer who used his fake identity while infiltrating serious crime to deceive a woman into a 19-year relationship during which they had a child together. Undercover police unit closed down over unjustified surveillance, spycops inquiry told Read more Victims of the surveillance say that the consultation is phoney and rigged as it only offers three alternatives: an inquiry with a narrower remit, one that would not have legal powers to force reluctant witnesses to testify or asking the police to disclose documents to victims without any type of inquiry. Kate Wilson, who was deceived into a two-year relationship by Kennedy , said: “Whatever the intentions of the Home Office in doing this, the practical effect of them curtailing the inquiry or reducing its powers to compel evidence will be a cover-up, and we may never understand the full extent of the misconduct that has occurred in undercover policing.” A Home Office spokesperson said: “The historic failings in undercover policing continue to shock the public. We are determined to get justice and hold those responsible to account. “However, the undercover policing inquiry was established more than a decade ago, and is yet to deliver justice for those affected, at significant cost to the taxpayer. It’s only right that we ask those affected themselves about the future of the inquiry.” Explore more on these topics Undercover police and policing Spycops scandal Police Surveillance Shabana Mahmood Home Office news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland
